title: Errands Before the March
premise: Play a young runner of the settlement at Fort Dearborn in the week the order to abandon the post arrives, August 1812: choose who hears it from you first, and where you are on the last nights before the gate opens.

opening.text:
JAUNT: ERRANDS BEFORE THE MARCH. Monday, 10 August 1812, at the mouth of the Chicago River. You are thirteen, you live in the settlement outside the pickets of Fort Dearborn, and you are the fastest pair of legs on the post: soldiers, traders and families all send you with their messages. The country has been at war with Britain since June. Last night an order came from the general at Detroit, and by this morning half the post has guessed what it says.

It is read on the parade today, and by noon everyone at the river mouth will know that the fort is to be given up. Who hears it from you first, and where you are on the last nights before the march, is up to you. The people and the places are real; the runner is you.

stops.text: 10 August 1812, morning, on the parade. General William Hull's order is read aloud: 'It is with regret I order the Evacuation of your Post owing to the want of Provisions'. The garrison is to go. The arms and ammunition are to be destroyed, and the goods in the government store handed out, some of them to 'the Poor & needy of your Post'. Wau-Bun says the officers' 'unanimous advice was, to remain where they were, and fortify themselves as strongly as possible.' They are overruled. Captain Heald will obey, and the men who argued with him will march out of the gate beside him. You heard all of it from the back of the crowd.
stops.narrative: Across the river, or out to the government houses?

choices.label: Across to the Kinzies'
choices.consequence: The trader who sells to the garrison should hear it first.

choices.label: Out to the Agency House
choices.consequence: The families sheltering there will want the news before anyone.

stops.text: Across the river and up the bank to the Kinzie house, 'the dwelling-house and trading-establishment of Mr. Kinzie', and 'The fort was situated on the southern bank, directly opposite this mansion'. Kinzie's trade with the garrison is a monopoly: in January Heald made 'Messrs. Kinzie & Forsyth' the fort's only sutlers. An abandoned post is a lost market, and a garrison that leaves takes its custom with it. It is family news as well: Lieutenant Helm's wife Margaret is the 'step-daughter of old John Kinzie'. The Kinzies will not march with the soldiers. When the day comes, they will go by boat.
stops.narrative: The trader's house across the river from the fort.

stops.text: West of the fort, the government's log houses: the factor's store, and beside it the Agency House, 'an old-fashioned log building, with a hall running through the centre'. Since April the people outside the pickets have 'intrenched themselves in the Agency House'. Its piazzas 'were planked up, for greater security, port-holes were cut, and sentinels posted at night.' Heald has enrolled 'fifteen militiamen from the civilian population outside the fort.' Behind the factor's door is the store the order gives away, down to the last blanket. By the end of the week the shelves will be bare.
stops.narrative: The planked-up house west of the fort.

stops.text: 12 August, afternoon, on the open ground west of the pickets. Heald wrote that the people of the country round 'came in from all quarters in order to receive the goods in the factory store, which they understood were to be given them.' Their leaders meet him here in council, and he promises them the goods. 'Captain Heald alone attended on the part of the military.' His officers will not stand with him. They take the blockhouses that overlook this ground, open the port-holes and point the cannon 'so as to command the whole assembly.' It is a promise made under the guns. What he means to do with the powder and the whiskey, he does not say.
stops.narrative: Where the work is tonight, or where the road comes in?

choices.label: Help with the night's work
choices.consequence: Something is to be carried after dark, and quiet hands are wanted.

choices.label: Watch the gate
choices.consequence: Whoever comes in next, you will see them first.

stops.text: 13 August, evening, above the fort's north-east corner. All day the factory store has been emptied: 'blankets, broadcloths, calicoes, paints'. Now comes the part of the bargain that was never spoken. 'The same evening the ammunition and liquor were carried, part into the sally-port, and thrown into a well which had been dug there to supply the garrison with water in case of emergency'. The muskets 'were broken up and thrown into the well'. The rest goes 'as secretly as possible through the northern gate, the heads of the barrels knocked in, and the contents poured into the river.' Heald feared they 'would make bad use of it'. You carry, and you keep quiet, and the knocking carries anyway.
stops.narrative: Where the barrels go down to the river.

stops.text: 14 August, sunset, at the main gate. The store is empty: Heald has given out its goods 'and a considerable quantity of provisions which we could not take away with us.' Captain William Wells rides in from Fort Wayne with his escort, Heald says 'about 30 Miamies'. Wells is Rebekah Heald's uncle, and he has come to bring her and her husband out. Wau-Bun says he came 'all too late': the ammunition is already destroyed. You saw him on the road before the sentry did. Tomorrow 'at 9 o'clock in the morning' the gate opens, and everyone inside walks out of it.
stops.narrative: The gate on the last evening.

legs.note: Out of the gate and across the river to the Kinzie house.
legs.story: Across the water with the news.

legs.note: Out of the gate and west to the government houses.
legs.story: West of the pickets, as fast as you can run.

legs.note: Back across the river and round to the open ground west of the fort.
A few steps north to the open ground below the north-west blockhouse.
Round the fort's north side to its north-east corner.
Round the fort to the main gate on its south side.

endings.text: By morning the water will taste of strong grog, and you know exactly why. You carried the order to the Kinzie house on the first day and rolled the barrels on the last night but one. On Saturday the garrison marches and the Kinzies go by boat. Whatever the fort leaves behind, there is nothing left in it to drink, and everyone outside the pickets knows it.

Your week began with news carried out of the fort and ends with news riding into it: the order to the Kinzie house, and Captain Wells through the gate at sunset, too late to change anything. Tonight nobody on the post is asleep. At nine tomorrow the band strikes up, the gate opens, and the column takes the beach with the lake on its left. The fort burns the morning after.

You told the Agency House first, and on the last night but one you helped make sure the fort would leave no powder and no whiskey behind it. The sentinels on the planked-up piazzas have one more night to stand. On Saturday at nine the garrison and the twelve militiamen march out, and the next morning, Heald wrote, 'they set fire to the fort and left the place'.

From the Agency House on the first morning to the gate at the last sunset, you carried the week's news on your own feet. Captain Wells is inside now, and the gates shut behind him for the last time. Tomorrow at nine they open, and the fort's week of waiting is over. Two days from now it will be ash; the army will come back in 1816 and build again on the same ground.

keepsake.title: A Runner's Week
keepsake.text: A made-up note of one young runner's errands in the week before the march of 15 August 1812: who heard the order first, and where the last nights were spent. No real runner or message is written on it.

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): 'Meanwhile war had been declared by Congress on June 18'. 'News of the declaration of war was received at Fort Dearborn toward the middle of July.'
evidence.locator: Quaife, the chapter on the evacuation (Gutenberg #69274 plain text, the paragraphs on Hull's march and on the news reaching Fort Dearborn)

evidence.text: General William Hull's order, Sandwich, 29 July 1812, found among the Heald papers and first printed by Quaife: 'It is with regret I order the Evacuation of your Post owing to the want of Provisions only a neglect of the Commandant' ... 'You will therefore Destroy all arms & ammunition, but the Goods of the Factory you may give to the Friendly Indians who may be desirous of Escorting you on to Fort Wayne & to the Poor & needy of your Post.'
evidence.locator: note 583, Gutenberg #69274 plain text, the evacuation chapter

evidence.text: Heald's journal: 'On the 9th of Augt, 1812, rec'd orders from Genl Wm. Hull to evacuate the Post of Chicago and proceed with my Command to Detroit.' Quaife: 'The next day the Indian runner. Winnemac, delivered to Captain Heald at Fort Dearborn his order for the evacuation.' Wau-Bun puts the runner, Winnemeg or Catfish, a Potawatomi, at the post on the 7th, bringing despatches that 'announced the declaration of war between the United States and Great Britain'. Wau-Bun: 'The order for evacuating the post was read next morning upon parade', and the officers' 'unanimous advice was, to remain where they were, and fortify themselves as strongly as possible.' Quaife defends Heald: 'Obedience to orders is the primary duty of a soldier.'
evidence.locator: Quaife Appendix III (Heald's journal) and the evacuation chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Heald's journal has the order received on 9 August; Wau-Bun says it 'was read next morning upon parade'. This stop is set on the morning of 10 August, putting the two together; the hour is Wau-Bun's 'next morning', not a recorded time.
evidence.reasoning: Heald's own date for the order's arrival plus Wau-Bun's 'next morning' for its reading; the two sources differ by two days on the runner, so the date is a reading, not a record.

evidence.text: Wau-Bun (1856): 'On the north side of the main stream, but quite near its junction with Lake Michigan, stood (as has already been described) the dwelling-house and trading-establishment of Mr. Kinzie.' 'The fort was situated on the southern bank, directly opposite this mansion'. The Chicago Reader (2018): in January 1812 Heald made 'Messrs. Kinzie & Forsyth' the exclusive fort sutlers. Kirkland (1893): Margaret Helm was the 'step-daughter of old John Kinzie'.
evidence.locator: Wau-Bun, the April section; the Reader, the sutler paragraph; Kirkland, the Helm narrative

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): 'after the murders at the Lee farm, Captain Heald enrolled fifteen militiamen from the civilian population outside the fort.' Wau-Bun: the people outside the fort 'now intrenched themselves in the Agency House'; its piazzas 'were planked up, for greater security, port-holes were cut, and sentinels posted at night.'
evidence.locator: Quaife, the chapter on the first fort (Gutenberg #69274 plain text, the paragraph on the civilians around the fort); Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): 'A short distance to the southwest were two log houses, one occupied by Matthew Irwin, the United States factor, and the other by Charles Jouett, the Indian agent.' Wau-Bun (1856) on the Agency House in April 1812: 'It was an old-fashioned log building, with a hall running through the centre, and one large room on each side. Piazzas extended the whole length of the building in front and rear. These were planked up, for greater security, port-holes were cut, and sentinels posted at night.'
evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. VI, the description of the fort (Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text, the paragraphs beginning 'There exist two contemporary pictures' and 'Within the stockaded inclosure'); Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text, the paragraph beginning 'It was an old-fashioned log building'

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'The neighboring Indians got the information as early as I did, and came in from all quarters in order to receive the goods in the factory store, which they understood were to be given them.' His warriors on the 15th were 'mostly of the Potawatamie nation' (the Potawatomi, as the name is now written). Wau-Bun puts a council on the afternoon of the 12th: 'Captain Heald alone attended on the part of the military.' His officers 'took command of the block-houses which overlooked the esplanade on which the council was held, opened the port-holes, and pointed the cannon so as to command the whole assembly.'
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Quaife note 589 and the evacuation chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'On the 14th, I delivered the Indians all the goods in the factory store, and a considerable quantity of provisions which we could not take away with us.' Wau-Bun, which dates it the 13th: 'the goods, consisting of blankets, broadcloths, calicoes, paints, etc., were distributed, as stipulated.'
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Wau-Bun puts the goods out on the 13th and the powder down the well 'The same evening', so the giving-out was by day; this stop is set at two in the afternoon of the 13th. No hour is recorded.
evidence.reasoning: Wau-Bun's sequence on the 13th (goods, then 'The same evening' the well); Heald dates the goods to the 14th. The hour is the jaunt's, inside the daylight the sequence needs.

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'The surplus arms and ammunition I thought proper to destroy, fearing they would make bad use of it if put in their possession. I also destroyed all the liquor on hand after they began to collect.' Wau-Bun: 'The same evening the ammunition and liquor were carried, part into the sally-port, and thrown into a well which had been dug there to supply the garrison with water in case of emergency; the remainder was transported as secretly as possible through the northern gate, the heads of the barrels knocked in, and the contents poured into the river.' The muskets 'were broken up and thrown into the well'. The noise betrayed it, and 'the taste of the water the next morning was, as one expressed it, "strong grog."'
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'On the 13th, Captain Wells, of Fort Wayne, arrived with about 30 Miamies, for the purpose of escorting us in, by the request of General Hull.' Wau-Bun has him arrive on the 14th 'with fifteen friendly Miamis' to save 'his relative, Captain Heald', and says he came 'all too late': the ammunition was already destroyed. Quaife: Heald's wife Rebekah was 'the niece of Captain Wells'.
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Quaife, the evacuation chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Wells reached the fort on the 13th by Heald's report or the 14th by Wau-Bun; Black Partridge came to the commanding officer 'on the evening' after the second council. This stop is set at sunset on 14 August, the eve of the march.
evidence.reasoning: Wau-Bun's 'evening succeeding the council' and the march next morning; the hour is a reading of 'evening'.

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'On the 15th, at 9 o'clock in the morning, we commenced our march: a part of the Miamies were detached in front, and the remainder in our rear, as guards, under the direction of Captain Wells. The situation of the country rendered it necessary for us to take the beach, with the lake on our left, and a high sand bank on our right, at about 100 yards distance.' Wau-Bun: 'As the troops left the fort, the band struck up the Dead March', and Wells 'had blackened his face before leaving the garrison, in token of his impending fate.' Mrs. Kinzie's boat 'had scarcely reached the mouth of the river, which, it will be recollected, was here half a mile below the fort, when another messenger from To-pee-nee-bee arrived to detain them where they were.' Quaife lists the order: Wells and part of the Miamis, the garrison, the women and children, the twelve Chicago militia.
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Quaife, the battle chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XIX, Narrative of the Massacre, Continued, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Heald's report, 23 October 1812: 'The next morning, they set fire to the fort and left the place, taking the prisoners with them.' Quaife (1913): 'over Chicago silence and desolation reigned supreme.' The second fort went up on the same ground in 1816.
evidence.locator: Quaife, Appendix IV, Heald's report; ch. IX, the paragraph beginning 'several villages'

evidence.text: The runner's calls at the Kinzie house and at the government houses west of the fort are set at eleven in the morning of 10 August 1812, after the order was read on parade that morning. No such call is recorded, and the hour is the jaunt's pacing.
evidence.reasoning: Heald's journal has the order received on 9 August and Wau-Bun has it read 'next morning upon parade'; a message carried from the parade to either house would arrive later the same morning. The hour is placed after the reading, not read from a source.

evidence.text: The runner the visitor plays, their age, their home outside the pickets and their errands, who sends them and where, the order of the route, the two choices, the four endings, the timing inputs and the A Runner's Week keepsake are invented connective narrative. No such runner is recorded. No child of a named family is played or met, nobody is put in danger by a choice, no named person speaks, and the walk ends on the eve of the march of 15 August 1812.
